title: How does an API Gateway handle caching, and what problems arise (stale data, granularity, caching sensitive data)?
shortTitle: How an API Gateway handles caching and what problems arise

s1_definition.profdef: Gateway caching stores the responses of safe, repeatable requests at the edge so that subsequent identical requests are served from the cache instead of hitting the backend. The gateway keys the cache on the request, usually method, path, query, and sometimes identity, respects HTTP cache-control directives, and applies a time-to-live. It cuts latency and backend load for read-heavy, slowly changing data. The main problems are stale data, where the cache serves data that has since changed; cache granularity, where the key is too coarse or too fine; and the serious risk of caching sensitive or personalized data and leaking it across users.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India front desk keeps a printed sheet of today's fixed-deposit interest rates. When any customer asks, the clerk hands over the sheet instantly instead of phoning the treasury department every time. That is caching, and it is wonderful for information that rarely changes. But problems appear: if the rates changed this morning and the sheet is from yesterday, the clerk gives wrong numbers, that is stale data. If the clerk accidentally keeps a copy of Rajesh's private balance on the shared desk and hands it to the next person, that is the disaster of caching sensitive, per-user data.
s1_definition.oneliner: Cache safe, shared, slowly changing reads at the gateway with a sensible TTL, and never cache per-user or sensitive data without strict per-identity keys and short expiry, or you will serve stale or leaked data.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Gateway caching stores the responses of safe, repeatable requests at the edge so that subsequent identical requests are served from the cache instead of hitting the backend. The gateway keys the cache on the request, usually method, path, query, and sometimes identity, respects HTTP cache-control directives, and applies a time-to-live. It cuts latency and backend load for read-heavy, slowly changing data. The main problems are stale data, where the cache serves data that has since changed; cache granularity, where the key is too coarse or too fine; and the serious risk of caching sensitive or personalized data and leaking it across users.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India front desk keeps a printed sheet of today's fixed-deposit interest rates. When any customer asks, the clerk hands over the sheet instantly instead of phoning the treasury department every time. That is caching, and it is wonderful for information that rarely changes. But problems appear: if the rates changed this morning and the sheet is from yesterday, the clerk gives wrong numbers, that is stale data. If the clerk accidentally keeps a copy of Rajesh's private balance on the shared desk and hands it to the next person, that is the disaster of caching sensitive, per-user data.

**One line to remember:** Cache safe, shared, slowly changing reads at the gateway with a sensible TTL, and never cache per-user or sensitive data without strict per-identity keys and short expiry, or you will serve stale or leaked data.

sections.s2_technical:
The gateway caches at the HTTP layer. It only caches idempotent, safe methods, almost always GET, because caching a POST that moves money would be catastrophic. Spring Cloud Gateway provides a `LocalResponseCache` filter and can also integrate with a distributed cache; the filter stores the response body and headers keyed by the request and serves it until it expires.

The cache key is the heart of correctness. A key that is too coarse, such as only the path, will serve one user's data to another if the response is personalized. A key that is too fine, such as including a timestamp or a random header, never gets a hit and the cache is useless. The right key includes method, path, and the query string, plus any header that changes the response meaning, and for personalized responses it must include the user identity, so Rajesh's cached data is never keyed the same as Priya's.

The gateway should honor HTTP caching semantics. A backend can return `Cache-Control: max-age=30` to say "safe to cache for thirty seconds", or `Cache-Control: no-store` to say "never cache this". A well-behaved gateway respects these so the service that owns the data controls its cacheability. It can also use validators like ETag and `If-None-Match` so the backend can cheaply confirm "still valid" with a 304 instead of resending the whole body.

Now the problems. Stale data is the fundamental trade-off: anything cached can be out of date for up to its TTL. For an account balance, even thirty seconds of staleness can confuse a customer who just made a transfer, so you either keep the TTL very short, cache only truly slow-changing data, or add active invalidation where the owning service tells the gateway to evict a key when the underlying data changes. Invalidation is famously hard in distributed systems because the gateway often does not know when the backend data changed.

Granularity problems come in two flavors. Over-caching treats dynamic or personalized responses as cacheable and serves wrong or leaked data. Under-caching sets keys so specific that nothing is reused and you pay the cost of a cache with none of the benefit. Finding the right key and TTL per endpoint is the real engineering work.

Caching sensitive data is the most dangerous problem. If the gateway caches a response containing Rajesh's balance under a key that does not include his identity, another user hitting the same path could receive his data. The rules are strict: never cache authenticated, user-specific responses in a shared cache without the user in the key; prefer `no-store` for anything sensitive; and never cache secrets, tokens, or PII at all. In banking this is also a compliance and audit concern.

A senior nuance is the distributed dimension. With several gateway replicas, a local per-replica cache can be inconsistent across replicas, so the same user might see fresh data from one replica and stale data from another. A shared cache like Redis fixes consistency but adds a network hop and becomes a shared dependency. The choice between local and distributed caching is a deliberate trade-off between speed, consistency, and coupling.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's app shows a "today's interest rates" panel to every customer. This data changes at most once a day and is identical for everyone, so calling the Rates Service on every app open is wasteful and slow. This is the perfect thing to cache at the gateway with a public key and a short TTL.

Problem 2 — The same gateway must not cache Rajesh's account balance under a shared path key, because then Priya opening her app could receive Rajesh's balance. And just after Rajesh transfers money, a cached balance would show the wrong number, confusing him. This shows the staleness and sensitive-data problems.

The connection to the fix: we will build a gateway cache that distinguishes cacheable public reads from non-cacheable or per-user reads. Public rates are cached with a TTL and shared across users. Account balances are either not cached or cached strictly per user with a very short TTL, and an explicit invalidation evicts the key after a transfer.

What the code will do. There is a `CacheKey` built from method, path, and optional user identity. There is a `GatewayCache` with put, get respecting TTL, and invalidate. There is a `CachingGateway` that decides per endpoint whether and how to cache, calling the backend on a miss. The demo requests the public rates twice to show a cache hit, requests two different users' balances to show per-user keying prevents leakage, and performs a transfer that invalidates Rajesh's cached balance.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a sequence of reads: the public rates twice, Rajesh's balance twice, Priya's balance once, then a transfer followed by Rajesh's balance again.

Step 1. The first rates request has a public policy and is cacheable with a sixty-second TTL. There is no entry, so it is a miss; the gateway calls the Rates Service, gets the rates, stores them under a public key, and returns them.

Step 2. The second rates request finds the public entry still within its TTL, so it is a hit served from the cache with no backend call. This is the pure win case: shared, slow-changing data served instantly.

Step 3. Rajesh's first balance request has a per-user policy with a five-second TTL. The key includes his identity, so it is a miss; the gateway calls the backend and caches the result under the key tagged with Rajesh. The second request hits that entry and returns his balance from the cache.

Step 4. Priya's balance request builds a different key, because her identity differs from Rajesh's. That key has no entry, so it is a miss and she gets her own balance from the backend. Because the key includes the user, Priya can never receive Rajesh's cached data, which is how per-user keying prevents leakage.

Step 5. A transfer completes for Rajesh. The gateway explicitly invalidates the cached balance key for Rajesh, removing the now-outdated entry. His next balance request is therefore a miss and fetches the fresh, correct balance from the backend. This active invalidation is what keeps sensitive, fast-changing data from going stale.

```
2026-10-24 13:30:01 [INFO] === Public rates (cacheable, shared) ===
2026-10-24 13:30:01 [INFO] CACHE MISS GET /api/v1/rates [public] → backend
2026-10-24 13:30:01 [INFO] CACHE HIT  GET /api/v1/rates [public]
2026-10-24 13:30:01 [INFO] === Per-user balance (sensitive, keyed by user) ===
2026-10-24 13:30:01 [INFO] CACHE MISS GET /api/v1/accounts/balance [user=rajesh] → backend
2026-10-24 13:30:01 [INFO] CACHE HIT  GET /api/v1/accounts/balance [user=rajesh]
2026-10-24 13:30:01 [INFO] CACHE MISS GET /api/v1/accounts/balance [user=priya] → backend
2026-10-24 13:30:01 [INFO] === Invalidation after a transfer ===
2026-10-24 13:30:01 [INFO] Transfer done for rajesh → invalidate cached balance
2026-10-24 13:30:01 [INFO] CACHE MISS GET /api/v1/accounts/balance [user=rajesh] → backend
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  GET request
    │
    ▼
  policyFor(path)
    ├─ /rates    → cacheable, public, TTL 60s
    ├─ /balance  → cacheable, PER-USER, TTL 5s
    └─ default   → NO-CACHE (always backend)
    │
    ▼
  build CacheKey(method, path, user?)
    │
    ▼
  GatewayCache.get(key)
    ├─ HIT (not expired) ──────→ return cached body (no backend call)
    └─ MISS / expired
           │
           ▼
      callBackend(path, user)
           │  store under key with TTL
           ▼
      return fresh body

  Transfer(rajesh) ──→ cache.invalidate(key for rajesh balance)
                        → next read = MISS = fresh
  Cross-user safety: key includes user → priya key ≠ rajesh key → no leak
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
An API Gateway caches at the HTTP layer by storing the responses of safe, repeatable requests, almost always GETs, keyed on the request and served until they expire. The benefit is obvious: for read-heavy, slowly changing data the gateway answers instantly without touching the backend, which cuts both latency and backend load. In my banking work at National Bank of India, the "today's interest rates" panel is identical for every customer and changes at most once a day, so we cache it at the gateway with a short TTL, and the vast majority of requests never reach the Rates Service.

The hard part is the cache key, because it decides correctness. A key that is too coarse, like just the path, will serve one customer's data to another if the response is personalized. A key that is too fine never gets a hit and the cache is pointless. For public data I key on method, path, and query. For personalized data I must include the user identity in the key, so Rajesh's balance and Priya's balance are stored under different keys and can never be confused. I also honor the backend's cache-control headers, so the service that owns the data decides whether and how long it may be cached.

The three problems I always call out are stale data, granularity, and sensitive data. Stale data is the built-in trade-off, because anything cached can be out of date for up to its TTL. Right after Rajesh transfers money, a cached balance would show the wrong number and confuse him, so for that data I keep the TTL very short and, more importantly, actively invalidate the cached balance the moment a transfer completes, which is the only reliable way to avoid serving a stale balance. Granularity is about picking the right key and TTL per endpoint so you neither over-cache dynamic data nor under-cache to the point of uselessness.

The most dangerous problem is caching sensitive or personalized data, because a wrong key can leak one customer's data to another, which in a bank is both a security breach and a compliance failure. My rules are firm: never cache authenticated, user-specific responses in a shared cache without the user in the key, prefer no-store for anything truly sensitive, and never cache tokens, secrets, or raw PII at all. Finally, I always flag the distributed angle, because with several gateway replicas a local per-replica cache can be inconsistent, so I choose deliberately between a fast local cache and a consistent shared cache like Redis, trading speed against consistency and coupling.
